catalogue.headline: Nine checks. Each one reads only what it needs.
catalogue.subhead: All nine run by default, on every document type. Seven read the whole thesis at once — that is how a term that quietly shifts meaning between chapters gets caught. Two read one page at a time.

citationStyle.name: Citation Style
citationStyle.description: Checks every in-text citation against the declared citation style and reports each deviation with the exact text that is wrong.

argumentation.name: Argumentation Analysis
argumentation.description: Examines whether claims are supported by evidence, whether the reasoning holds, and where an argument is asserted rather than shown.

coherence.name: Coherence
coherence.description: Assesses whether the thesis flows as a single line of thought — transitions, referential clarity, and sections that contradict one another.

logicalErrors.name: Logical Errors
logicalErrors.description: Page-by-page detection of formal and informal fallacies: non sequiturs, circular reasoning, false dilemmas and overgeneralisation.

coverPage.name: Cover Page
coverPage.description: Verifies the title page carries every element a university requires and that nothing is missing or malformed.

chapterOrder.name: Chapter Order
chapterOrder.description: Compares the table of contents against the actual chapter sequence and flags numbering gaps, mismatches and structural omissions.

gendering.name: Gendering & Inclusivity
gendering.description: Page-by-page review of gendered and exclusionary language, applying the conventions of the document’s own language variant.

terminology.name: Terminology
terminology.description: Finds terms used inconsistently, defined late or never, or silently shifting meaning between chapters.

sourceDensity.name: Source Density
sourceDensity.description: Locates passages making substantive claims with too little citation support, and passages so dense with citation they lack the author’s own voice.

defense.headline: Answer it badly in private, not in the viva.
defense.subhead: Scriptor generates the questions your committee is most likely to ask, drawn from what your text actually claims. You answer them, get scored, and answer again — and every attempt is kept, so you can see the answer getting better.
defense.question: You treat self-reported productivity and manager assessment as equivalent measures. What would change in your conclusions if they diverged?

a.label: 1st
a.answer: I think they measure broadly similar things, so the conclusions would probably still hold. The literature I reviewed treats them more or less interchangeably.
a.feedback: You restate the assumption the question is challenging. The examiner already knows the literature conflates them — they are asking you to defend doing it, not to repeat that it is done.

b.label: 2nd
b.answer: They could diverge if managers reward visibility rather than output. That would inflate manager scores for on-site staff and depress them for remote staff.
b.feedback: Better — you name a mechanism instead of asserting equivalence. Now finish it: say what that mechanism does to your finding. Does the effect shrink, vanish, or reverse?

c.label: 3rd
c.answer: They diverge precisely where my claim is strongest. If managers reward visibility, the remote cohort is systematically under-scored, so my measured effect is a floor rather than an estimate — and Chapter 5 should therefore be stated as directional, not as a magnitude.
c.feedback: Strong. You name the mechanism, its direction, and what it costs the claim, then adjust the claim rather than defending it whole. This is a defensible answer.

faq.headline: The things you actually want to know before uploading a year of work.
faq.subhead: No hedging. Where the answer is a limitation, it says so.

a.q: Is my thesis used to train anything?
a.a: No. Sharing is off by default and stays off unless you deliberately turn it on for an upload. Your file sits in a private bucket — no public link to it exists anywhere, and the only way to open it is a short-lived signed URL created for your session.

b.q: Can anyone else read my thesis?
b.a: No. Ownership is enforced in the database, not just hidden in the interface: every row carries the account it belongs to, and there is no query — from the app or otherwise — that returns another person’s paper. Your supervisor cannot see it unless you show them.

c.q: How long do you keep my file?
c.a: The source document is deleted 90 days after upload by default, and a scheduled sweep removes it from storage as well as from the database. You can switch that off for a particular upload, or change the default for your account in settings.

d.a: Yes, and it cascades. Deleting a paper removes its pages, its per-word data, every finding, every reference and the stored file itself. Nothing is kept behind for analytics.

a.a: A PDF or a Word document, up to 50 MB. Anything longer than the limit for your document type is rejected before any analysis starts, so you are told immediately rather than after a long wait.

b.q: Which citation styles do you know?
b.a: Ten: APA 6 and 7, MLA 9, Chicago 17, Harvard, Vancouver, Oxford, Turabian, IEEE and ISO 690. Citations are checked against the style your document declares, so a citation that is correct in a different style still counts as a deviation.

c.q: What if a check fails halfway through?
c.a: It retries, waiting longer each time, so a brief provider outage does not lose your analysis. Optional extras are separated from the core: if defense questions or AI detection never succeed, your grammar and citation results still complete and are still shown.

d.a: Nothing at the moment. Scriptor is still in development, there is no billing, and every feature is switched on for every upload. When that changes it will be announced rather than quietly introduced.
